1.referenceTitle: Organic production standards without heavy-metal occurrence monitoring
1.citation: U.S. Department of Agriculture. National Organic Program, 7 CFR Part 205, current text reviewed September 15, 2026; European Parliament and Council. Regulation (EU) 2018/848 of May 30, 2018 on organic production and labelling of organic products. Official Journal L 150, June 14, 2018, pp. 1–92 (original act).
1.summary: These U.S. and EU rules govern organic production, permitted substances, certification and controls. Neither is a general finished-food lead, cadmium, arsenic and mercury concentration specification.
1.establishes: Organic certification is not proof that a particular product meets a separate metal specification. Both frameworks nevertheless require precautions and compliance controls; organic status does not exempt food from other food-safety law.
1.relevance: This distinction supports HMTc requiring analytical evidence in addition to an organic label. It does not establish that organic certification ignores contamination or authorizes food above applicable legal limits.

2.referenceTitle: Lead and cadmium contamination in a large sample of United States infant formulas and baby foods
2.citation: Gardener H, Bowen J, Callan SP. Lead and cadmium contamination in a large sample of United States infant formulas and baby foods. Science of the Total Environment. 2019;651:822–827. Published online September 4, 2018. doi:10.1016/j.scitotenv.2018.09.026.
2.summary: This convenience survey tested 564 U.S. retail and online infant-formula and baby-food products by ICP-MS. Label-based organic groups included 304 organic and 260 nonorganic products.
2.establishes: Organic status was not significantly associated with cadmium (p=0.65) or lead (p=0.28). Grain ingredients, especially rice, were associated with higher concentrations. Each product was purchased and tested once; sampling was not nationally representative.
2.relevance: The results support checking measured contamination rather than assuming an organic label predicts these metals. Statistical nulls in this sample do not prove equivalence or quantify the effect of choosing organic rice cereal.

3.referenceTitle: Assessment of Essential Elements and Potentially Toxic Elements (PTEs) in Organic and Conventional Flaxseeds: Implications for Dietary Exposure and Food Safety
3.citation: Brum R de L, Siedzik K, Alejandro-Vega S, et al. Assessment of Essential Elements and Potentially Toxic Elements (PTEs) in Organic and Conventional Flaxseeds: Implications for Dietary Exposure and Food Safety. Applied Sciences. 2025;15(13):7004. Published June 21, 2025. doi:10.3390/app15137004.
3.summary: The researchers measured 20 elements by ICP-OES in 52 commercially obtained European-market flaxseed samples, classified as 15 organic and 37 conventional.
3.establishes: Lead and cadmium differences were not statistically significant. Organic samples had lower aluminium and nickel (p=0.0312 and 0.0142), while sodium was higher. These observational group comparisons did not isolate farming practice from origin or other supply-chain differences.
3.relevance: The matrix-specific findings support HMTc measuring individual elements. They do not establish universal equivalence between farming systems or validate any HMTc limit or exposure-reduction claim.

4.referenceTitle: A multi-year heavy metal analysis of 72 dark chocolate and cocoa products in the USA
4.citation: Hands JM, Anderson ML, Cooperman T, Balsky JE, Frame LA. A multi-year heavy metal analysis of 72 dark chocolate and cocoa products in the USA. Frontiers in Nutrition. 2024;11:1366231. Published July 31, 2024. doi:10.3389/fnut.2024.1366231.
4.summary: This observational ConsumerLab-derived survey measured 72 product observations across 2014, 2016, 2019 and 2022. The full-sample concentration medians were 50 µg/kg lead and 239 µg/kg cadmium.
4.establishes: The organic cadmium comparison in Table 4 used 37 observations with daily-intake data: 15 organic and 22 nonorganic. Organic products were higher by a one-tailed Welch test (p≈0.02). Geography and blending were not measured explanations.
4.relevance: This supports separate metal measurements for chocolate carrying organic claims. It does not show that certification caused the difference or that organic single-origin versus conventional West African blending explains it.

5.referenceTitle: Assessment of cadmium and lead content in tomatoes and tomato products
5.citation: Grochowska-Niedworok E, Nieć J, Baranowska R. Assessment of cadmium and lead content in tomatoes and tomato products. Roczniki Państwowego Zakładu Higieny. 2020;71(3):313–319. doi:10.32394/rpzh.2020.0126.
5.summary: This Polish retail study used graphite-furnace atomic absorption spectrometry to measure lead and cadmium in different tomato varieties and processed products, reporting fresh- and dry-mass results.
5.establishes: Several organic dry-mass samples had higher cadmium than some conventional varieties, but the study was not a matched or statistically adjusted farming-system comparison. An organic fresh Jawor tomato had both metals below quantification. The authors reported one canned concentrate above their chosen cadmium benchmark.
5.relevance: The findings illustrate product variability relevant to HMTc testing. They cannot establish a general organic penalty or identify the concentrate exceedance as an organic product.

6.referenceTitle: Chemical Composition and Nutritional Quality of Commercial Tahini
6.citation: Potortì AG, Albergamo A, Nava V, Lo Turco V, Litrenta F, Spanò IM, Di Bella G. Chemical Composition and Nutritional Quality of Commercial Tahini. Applied Sciences. 2026;16(3):1400. Published January 29, 2026. doi:10.3390/app16031400.
6.summary: The study examined seven Italian-market tahini brands purchased online in 2025, using three analytical replicates per product. Table 1 identifies two organic products: T-1 from Turkey and T-5 from Lebanon.
6.establishes: T-1 contained cadmium 0.35, lead 0.50 and total arsenic 0.20 mg/kg; T-5 had cadmium 0.02, lead 0.01 and arsenic below quantification. Seven products cannot isolate an organic effect. The authors compared tahini to limits for other food categories.
6.relevance: The contrast between these two organic products reinforces HMTc’s need for product-specific measurements. It does not establish that organic tahini is generally higher or independently prove a regulatory violation.

7.referenceTitle: Assessment of Heavy Metals in Organic and Non-Organic Vegetables Post Severe Tropical Cyclone Gabrielle: A cross-sectional comparative analysis.
7.citation: Dearing, Chey; Ye, Zhijing; and Robertshaw, Glen. Assessment of Heavy Metals in Organic and Non-Organic Vegetables Post Severe Tropical Cyclone Gabrielle: A cross-sectional comparative analysis. F1000Research 14:1461 (26 December 2025), version 1, awaiting peer review in the examined version. doi:10.12688/f1000research.175538.1.
7.summary: This cross-sectional study tested 153 composite samples made from 736 vegetables bought at 14 Hawke’s Bay market gardens in February 2024. Its main analysis associated organic production with lower cadmium and nickel, and the authors reported four composite samples above their selected Codex limits.
7.establishes: The observations are local and do not establish a fertilizer mechanism or certification guarantee. Lead and arsenic were excluded from comparative statistical analysis because most results were below detection limits. In a 37-sample sensitivity analysis restricted by vegetable type, only nickel retained a significant organic association.
7.relevance: This local survey shows that measured metals can vary with production setting and vegetable mix. It supports HMTc seeking laboratory evidence, while its lower organic cadmium result and statistical limitations prevent a universal claim that organic certification cannot be protective.

8.relevance: It provides a source map for this HMTc article. Its interpretations must be checked against the underlying studies; common authorship and Paleo-related operation mean a separate website alone does not establish independent corroboration.

1.referenceTitle: Hain Celestial Group, Inc. v. Palmquist
1.citation: Supreme Court of the United States. Hain Celestial Group, Inc. v. Palmquist, No. 24-724, 607 U.S. ___ (2026), unanimous opinion by Justice Sotomayor, 24 February 2026.
1.summary: The Court affirmed that erroneous dismissal of a retailer whose citizenship defeated federal diversity jurisdiction did not cure the jurisdictional defect. The manufacturer’s favorable federal judgment therefore could not stand.
1.establishes: This procedural holding does not decide injury causation, product defects or certification. Properly curing a jurisdictional defect remains different from wrongly dismissing a party; the decision does not prohibit all retailer dismissals or require a jury trial after every remand.
1.relevance: It supplies the legal event behind this briefing’s emphasis on records that can be examined in different courts. Predictions about widespread state-court trials, greater settlement pressure and certification’s economic value are the author’s analysis, not court findings.

2.referenceTitle: Palmquist v. Hain Celestial Group, Inc.
2.citation: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit. Palmquist v. Hain Celestial Group, Inc., No. 23-40197, opinion by Judge Carl E. Stewart, 28 May 2024.
2.summary: The Fifth Circuit found that the pleaded claims against Whole Foods supported remand, vacated the federal judgment and directed return to state court. Its factual background also describes Hain’s testing history.
2.establishes: The federal win was judgment as a matter of law under Rule 50 after the plaintiffs rested, not a defense jury verdict. The appellate court resolved jurisdiction and expressly did not decide whether the merits judgment was correct.
2.relevance: It explains the procedural cost of litigating in a court without jurisdiction. Its account of Hain beginning finished-product testing in 2019 provides context for the briefing’s recordkeeping argument, but does not establish that a testing narrative replaces proof of causation.

6.establishes: All four statutory conditions matter. Routine surveillance can help establish some conditions, but neither an HMTc seal nor creation before litigation establishes the entire foundation. A California venue alone does not make this state rule govern a federal MDL.
6.relevance: The provision is relevant when HMTc testing records are offered in a proceeding governed by California evidence law. It supports documenting the record’s origin and preparation without promising admission or assuming identical rules across state and federal cases.

7.citation: Federal Rules of Evidence, Rule 901(a), (b)(1), (b)(9); see Rule 902(11). Official compilation, 1 December 2025. ISO/IEC 17025:2017, General requirements for the competence of testing and calibration laboratories, third edition, November 2017.
7.summary: Rule 901 requires evidence sufficient to support that an item is what its proponent claims. Examples include a knowledgeable witness and evidence explaining an accurate process or system. ISO/IEC 17025 separately provides a laboratory-competence and impartiality benchmark.

Authentication also does not establish the truth of every result, resolve hearsay objections or prevent cross-examination.
7.relevance: The sources explain why HMTc should preserve sample identity, handling records and laboratory methods. Whether a particular report is authenticated remains a legal and factual question; the program’s rule invalidating a result after a custody break is not an automatic court exclusion rule.

Three Journal of Food Metallomics preprints: The Counterproductive Consequences of Public Exposé Testing: How Unstructured Disclosure Undermines Heavy Metal Contamination Reduction (8 April 2026), doi:10.5281/zenodo.19470572; The Cost of Operating Without Credible Third-Party Heavy-Metal Certification (7 March 2026), doi:10.5281/zenodo.18903738; and Certification as a Framework for Reducing Heavy Metal Exposure in Infant and Child Foods: Integrating Legal Defensibility, Scientific Rigor, and Commercial Viability (8 March 2026), doi:10.5281/zenodo.18905821.

3.referenceTitle: General Requirements for the Competence of Testing and Calibration Laboratories
3.citation: International Organization for Standardization and International Electrotechnical Commission. ISO/IEC 17025:2017, General requirements for the competence of testing and calibration laboratories. Third edition, November 2017; confirmed in 2023.
3.summary: ISO/IEC 17025 sets a common benchmark for laboratory competence, impartiality and consistent operation. Accreditation bodies use the standard when assessing testing and calibration laboratories.

1.referenceTitle: Baby Foods Are Tainted with Dangerous Levels of Arsenic, Lead, Cadmium, and Mercury
1.citation: U.S. House Committee on Oversight and Reform, Subcommittee on Economic and Consumer Policy. Staff report, 4 February 2021.
1.summary: Congressional staff reviewed manufacturers’ testing records and reported arsenic, lead, cadmium and mercury contamination in baby foods, alongside weaknesses in testing and internal company limits.
1.establishes: The report recommended finished-product testing, regulatory limits and public disclosure. It was an investigation of company records, not an independent testing study or an enacted safety standard.
1.relevance: It provides context for HMTc’s emphasis on finished-product verification and the familiar four-metal panel. Its scope does not establish that only those four elements warrant testing.

2.referenceTitle: Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915 on maximum levels for certain contaminants in food
2.citation: European Commission. Regulation (EU) 2023/915, 25 April 2023. Original act, OJ L 119, 5 May 2023; Annex I, section 3.5.
2.summary: This regulation consolidates EU maximum contaminant levels for specified foods. Its metal provisions include inorganic tin in canned products, alongside lead, cadmium, arsenic and mercury.
2.establishes: The original act sets binding tin limits that distinguish general canned foods, beverages and specified infant foods. The applicable food category and exclusions matter; it is not a universal limit for all foods.
2.relevance: It provides a regulatory basis for including tin in HMTc’s coverage and matching limits to product and packaging. Applying a category’s limit elsewhere requires a separate, disclosed HMTc decision.

3.referenceTitle: Commission Regulation (EU) 2024/1987 amending Regulation (EU) 2023/915 as regards maximum levels of nickel in food
3.citation: European Commission. Regulation (EU) 2024/1987, 30 July 2024. Published 31 July 2024; Annex, section 3.6.
3.summary: This amendment introduces nickel maximum levels for specified foods in response to EFSA’s assessment of dietary exposure and health risks.
3.establishes: The legal limits distinguish food categories, including powdered formula, qualifying soy-isolate formula and liquid formula. Most apply from July 2025, with specified cereal provisions applying from July 2026.
3.relevance: This is the concentration-limit source behind the briefing’s inclusion of nickel and its formula distinctions. EFSA’s assessment in reference 7 explains the health rationale; this regulation supplies the food-specific legal requirements.

4.referenceTitle: Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code — Schedule 19, Maximum levels of contaminants and natural toxicants
4.citation: Food Standards Australia New Zealand. Schedule 19, compilation 6, 13 September 2024; infant-formula changes under Proposal P1028.
4.summary: Schedule 19 includes tin limits for canned foods and separate aluminium limits for infant-formula categories, extending food-contaminant controls beyond the conventional four metals.
4.establishes: The aluminium entries distinguish general, soy-based and specified preterm formula. The revised infant-formula rules apply in Australia with transition arrangements through September 2029; New Zealand opted out of those revisions.
4.relevance: These provisions support considering aluminium and tin in HMTc’s panel. Any use of the formula benchmark in another category must identify the jurisdiction, edition, preparation basis and rationale for that application.

5.citation: California Assembly Bill 899. Chapter 668, Statutes of 2023, approved 10 October 2023; Health and Safety Code sections 110962–110963.
5.summary: AB 899 requires covered baby-food manufacturers to test finished products for arsenic, cadmium, lead and mercury at least monthly, and to disclose product results publicly.
5.establishes: Testing began in January 2024 and public disclosure in January 2025. The law covers specified foods for children under two, excludes infant formula, and does not itself set numerical maximum metal concentrations.
5.relevance: It is a concrete example of a mandatory four-element disclosure panel. HMTc’s broader testing scope is a program decision; the law’s four-element list does not establish that other metals are irrelevant.

6.referenceTitle: Action Levels for Lead in Processed Food Intended for Babies and Young Children: Guidance for Industry
6.citation: U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Final guidance for industry, January 2025, issued 6 January 2025.
6.summary: FDA’s Closer to Zero guidance sets lead action levels for specified processed foods marketed for children under two, with different levels for different food categories.
6.establishes: These action levels inform FDA’s decisions about adulteration alongside other evidence. They are nonbinding recommendations, not universal safety thresholds; infant formula, beverages and snacks such as puffs are outside this guidance’s scope.
6.relevance: The guidance supports HMTc’s use of category-specific controls and careful identification of regulatory scope. It addresses lead in the named foods, rather than establishing a comprehensive metal-testing panel.

7.referenceTitle: Update of the Risk Assessment of Nickel in Food and Drinking Water
7.citation: EFSA CONTAM Panel. EFSA Journal 2020;18(11):6268, published 5 November 2020. DOI: 10.2903/j.efsa.2020.6268.
7.summary: EFSA reassessed dietary nickel using updated toxicology and food-occurrence data. It identified concerns for children with high exposure and for people already sensitized to nickel.
7.establishes: The chronic intake benchmark rests on reproductive effects in rats. High dietary exposure raised concern in young age groups, while acute oral exposure can provoke eczema in sensitized people. These are distinct health endpoints, not interchangeable thresholds.
7.relevance: This assessment provides the dietary-health rationale for including nickel in HMTc’s panel. The food concentration limits and formula distinctions discussed in the briefing come from the separate EU regulation in reference 3.

8.referenceTitle: IARC Monographs on the Identification of Carcinogenic Hazards to Humans
8.citation: International Agency for Research on Cancer. Monographs, volume 49 (1990) and volume 100C (2012); nickel chapter, volume 100C, pp. 169–218.
8.summary: IARC evaluates carcinogenic hazards using human, animal and mechanistic evidence. These volumes cover nickel compounds and other metals relevant to the briefing.
8.establishes: Nickel compounds are classified as carcinogenic to humans. The human evidence concerns lung and nasal cancers in occupationally exposed populations; the classification does not quantify cancer risk from eating nickel-containing foods.
8.relevance: The monographs provide hazard context for HMTc’s panel and show why chemical form and exposure route matter. Dietary nickel risk is addressed more directly by EFSA in reference 7; an IARC classification does not set a food limit.

9.referenceTitle: General Standard for Contaminants and Toxins in Food and Feed (CXS 193-1995), tin maximum levels
9.citation: Codex Alimentarius Commission (FAO/WHO). General Standard for Contaminants and Toxins in Food and Feed, CXS 193-1995, amended 2025; tin provisions.
9.summary: Codex’s general contaminant standard includes maximum tin levels for canned foods and canned beverages, with the two categories treated separately.
9.establishes: Tin is an established food-contaminant concern in international standards. These are commodity-specific Codex levels; they do not automatically become domestic law or apply to every food.
9.relevance: This supports HMTc’s inclusion of tin beyond the four-metal convention and its attention to packaging. HMTc must still compare applicable national requirements and select the correct product category when deriving a limit.

10.referenceTitle: Evaluation of Certain Food Additives and Contaminants (aluminium; tin)
10.citation: JECFA. Aluminium: 74th meeting, WHO TRS 966 (2011). Tin: 33rd meeting (1988), TRS 776 (1989); later clarification at the 64th meeting (2005), TRS 930 (2006).
10.summary: This reference combines separate assessments. Aluminium is evaluated through cumulative dietary intake; tin’s principal canned-food concern is acute gastrointestinal irritation.
10.establishes: The aluminium evaluation derives a provisional weekly intake benchmark. Later tin evaluations emphasize that irritation depends on the concentration and nature of tin in the product, and can occur around existing canned-product limits in some people.
10.relevance: These assessments support treating aluminium exposure and tin contamination differently within HMTc. They do not independently establish HMTc’s aluminium limits for other food categories, or make an elevated tin result a definitive diagnosis of can failure.

11.referenceTitle: Scientific Opinion: Safety of Aluminium from Dietary Intake
11.citation: EFSA AFC Panel. EFSA Journal 2008;6(7):754, pp. 1–34, published 15 July 2008. DOI: 10.2903/j.efsa.2008.754.
11.summary: EFSA assessed aluminium exposure from food, accounting for its persistence in the body and adverse effects observed in animal studies. Estimated dietary exposure could exceed its tolerable intake in part of the European population.
11.establishes: The opinion sets a health-based reference for total weekly dietary exposure. It addresses cumulative intake, rather than prescribing a maximum aluminium concentration for an individual food.
11.relevance: It explains why aluminium warrants attention in HMTc’s broader panel. Deriving an HMTc product limit still requires a separate rationale that connects exposure, food category and the chosen regulatory benchmark.

12.referenceTitle: IRIS Toxicological Review of Hexavalent Chromium [Cr(VI)]
12.citation: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. EPA/635/R-24/164Fa, August 2024; released 12 August 2024.
12.summary: EPA reviewed the cancer and noncancer effects of hexavalent chromium and concluded that it is likely to be carcinogenic to humans through oral exposure.
12.establishes: The assessment characterizes hazards and dose-response relationships specifically for Cr(VI). Its oral noncancer reference dose rests on small-intestine effects in mice; it is not a food concentration limit or an assessment of total chromium as one substance.
12.relevance: It supports distinguishing chromium species when HMTc interprets a total-chromium result. The choice of a screening trigger and the resulting certification decision remain HMTc program rules with their own justification.

13.referenceTitle: EFSA CONTAM Panel scientific opinions on lead, arsenic, mercury, and cadmium in food
13.summary: These five opinions assess dietary exposure and critical health effects for lead, inorganic arsenic, mercury species and cadmium. They are separate assessments with different endpoints and methods.
13.establishes: Lead and inorganic arsenic are assessed using benchmark reference points and exposure comparisons; mercury and cadmium have tolerable weekly intakes. Chemical form matters, particularly for arsenic and mercury.
13.relevance: The opinions support retaining the original four contaminants within HMTc’s broader panel and identifying relevant chemical species. They provide the scientific basis for concern, while HMTc separately defines its tiers, product limits and certification rules.

14.citation: NSF/ANSI 173-2025, Dietary Supplements. NSF / American National Standards Institute.
14.summary: NSF/ANSI 173 addresses dietary-supplement identity, declared composition and contaminants. NSF’s public certification description names lead, arsenic, cadmium, mercury and chromium(VI) among the toxic contaminants evaluated.
14.establishes: This is a documented supplement-certification comparator whose published screening scope extends beyond the familiar four metals. The public scope description identifies contaminants, rather than supplying the full standard’s numerical requirements.
14.relevance: It gives HMTc a specific basis for comparing the contaminants named by another program. Claims of unique or broader market coverage require a separate, current comparison of all relevant programs.

15.referenceTitle: ICH Q3D Guideline for Elemental Impurities; USP General Chapter <232>
15.citation: ICH Q3D(R2), adopted 26 April 2022. USP General Chapter <232>, Elemental Impurities—Limits; implementation FAQ, 27 March 2015 (chapter revision unspecified).
15.summary: ICH Q3D provides a risk-based framework and permitted daily exposures for elemental impurities in drug products. USP chapter <232> addresses elemental-impurity limits in that pharmaceutical context.
15.establishes: ICH’s table overlaps seven Big 8 element names and omits an aluminium exposure limit. Its default chromium assessment concerns Cr(III), with Cr(VI) requiring separate consideration; listed elements do not all require testing in every product.
15.relevance: The pharmaceutical framework offers a comparison of scope and exposure-based limits. Its element-name overlap is not equivalent to HMTc’s chemical-species coverage, food standards or testing requirements.

1.referenceTitle: Proposition 65 List of Chemicals Known to the State to Cause Cancer or Reproductive Toxicity
1.citation: California OEHHA. The Proposition 65 List. Current online chemical list, accessed September 15, 2026.
1.summary: California lists particular chemical forms and endpoints, including lead, cadmium, inorganic arsenic, hexavalent chromium and nickel compounds. Soluble nickel compounds were listed for developmental and male reproductive toxicity on October 26, 2018.
1.establishes: Listing identifies a statutory hazard; it supplies neither a food concentration limit nor proof that every exposure causes harm. Different forms of a metal have different listed endpoints.
1.relevance: The list supports the briefing’s hazard-identification premise. HMTc’s decision to impose product limits remains a separate program choice.

2.referenceTitle: Safe Drinking Water and Toxic Enforcement Act of 1986 (Proposition 65)
2.citation: California Health and Safety Code §§25249.5–25249.14. Safe Drinking Water and Toxic Enforcement Act of 1986; operative January 1, 1987, as amended.
2.summary: The Act requires qualifying businesses to warn before covered exposures and separately restricts releases into drinking-water sources. It provides exposure-based exemptions, enforcement and a chemical-listing process.
2.establishes: Its warning provisions do not create general food-composition ceilings. Section 25249.13 preserves other legal obligations: a warning does not authorize sale of any concentration under all food laws.
2.relevance: This supports a limited distinction between warning compliance and HMTc product specifications. The briefing’s claim that the Act does only one thing omits its discharge prohibition.

3.referenceTitle: Proposition 65 Safe Harbor Levels — No Significant Risk Levels and Maximum Allowable Dose Levels
3.citation: California OEHHA. Proposition 65 No Significant Risk Levels (NSRLs) and Maximum Allowable Dose Levels (MADLs). Current online safe-harbor table, accessed September 15, 2026.
3.summary: The table lists daily-exposure safe harbors. Lead has a 15 µg/day oral NSRL and 0.5 µg/day MADL; cadmium and hexavalent chromium have oral MADLs of 4.1 and 8.2 µg/day.
3.establishes: Inorganic arsenic has a 10 µg/day NSRL except by inhalation, directly contradicting the briefing’s assertion that it has no oral safe harbor. These exposure values are not food concentrations or universal safety assurances.
3.relevance: HMTc must distinguish a product’s concentration from the resulting daily exposure and the applicable chemical form and endpoint when comparing its limits with Proposition 65.

4.referenceTitle: Nickel and Nickel Compounds — Proposition 65 Warnings Website fact sheet
4.citation: California OEHHA. Nickel and Nickel Compounds. Proposition 65 Warnings Website fact sheet, posted February 2025.
4.summary: The fact sheet explains nickel cancer listings and the developmental effects of soluble nickel compounds and nickel carbonyl. It also identifies male reproductive effects for soluble nickel compounds.
4.establishes: This is a public hazard-and-exposure explanation, not an adopted oral dose limit. The separate safe-harbor table contains only the two specified nickel cancer entries and no general oral nickel MADL.
4.relevance: It supports the briefing’s concern about dietary nickel while leaving any numerical HMTc product specification to a separately documented standard.

5.referenceTitle: Evidence on the Developmental and Reproductive Toxicity of Nickel and Nickel Compounds
5.citation: California OEHHA. Evidence on the Developmental and Reproductive Toxicity of Nickel and Nickel Compounds. Hazard identification document, July 2018.
5.summary: The executive summary reviews human associations and animal evidence. Reduced offspring survival and body weight were common sensitive effects in prenatal animal studies, most of which used oral exposure.
5.establishes: The review supports hazard identification; it does not adopt a dietary safe harbor, a food maximum or a finding that ordinary dietary nickel causes these outcomes in children.
5.relevance: It explains the scientific concern underlying the briefing’s nickel discussion. Converting that concern into an HMTc concentration limit requires additional exposure assumptions and program rules.

6.referenceTitle: Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915 on maximum levels for certain contaminants in food
6.citation: European Commission. Regulation (EU) 2023/915 of April 25, 2023 on maximum levels for certain contaminants in food. OJ L 119, May 5, 2023, pp. 103–157; consolidated text dated August 19, 2026 consulted.
6.summary: Article2 bars listed foods exceeding applicable Annex I limits from the market and from ingredient use. The Annex sets category-specific limits for lead, cadmium, arsenic and inorganic tin; the amended framework also includes nickel.
6.establishes: These are EU concentration limits with defined food categories and measurement bases. They are not automatically US law. The consolidated text is a documentation aid; authentic amending acts remain controlling.
6.relevance: This supports using EU limits as a distinct benchmark. It does not establish that HMTc adopts every strictest limit or applies the correct category in every lot decision.

7.referenceTitle: Commission Regulation (EU) 2024/1987 amending (EU) 2023/915 as regards maximum levels of nickel in food
7.citation: European Commission. Regulation (EU) 2024/1987 of July 30, 2024 amending Regulation (EU) 2023/915 as regards maximum levels of nickel in certain foodstuffs. OJ L2024/1987, July 31, 2024.
7.summary: The amendment adds category-specific nickel maxima, including nuts, vegetables, cereals, chocolate, formula and baby food. It generally applies from July 1, 2025; specified cereal entries apply from July 1, 2026.
7.establishes: The limits are binding EU rules, with product-specific measurement bases and protection for food lawfully marketed before the applicable dates until its durability/use-by date. They are not a single daily-intake limit.
7.relevance: This supplies a concrete regulatory benchmark for HMTc’s nickel discussion, while requiring the correct food category and transition rule.

8.referenceTitle: Update of the Risk Assessment of Nickel in Food and Drinking Water
8.citation: EFSA CONTAM Panel. Update of the risk assessment of nickel in food and drinking water. EFSA Journal. 2020;18(11):6268. doi:10.2903/j.efsa.2020.6268.
8.summary: EFSA derived a chronic tolerable daily intake of 13 µg/kg body weight from rat post-implantation loss, using a 100-fold uncertainty factor. Higher-percentile dietary exposure often exceeded it in young groups.
8.establishes: Mean exposure was generally below or near the TDI; the study does not show all ordinary European diets exceed it. A TDI covers total intake per body weight, not the permitted concentration of one food.
8.relevance: The assessment informs HMTc’s rationale for considering nickel, but cannot itself supply a product limit without assumptions about consumption and other sources.

9.referenceTitle: Cadmium in food — Scientific Opinion of the Panel on Contaminants in the Food Chain
9.citation: EFSA CONTAM Panel. Cadmium in food. EFSA Journal. 2009;7(3):980,1–139. Adopted January 30, 2009; published March 20, 2009. doi:10.2903/j.efsa.2009.980.
9.summary: EFSA established a tolerable weekly intake of 2.5 µg/kg body weight, using kidney-effect biomarkers and exposure modelling. Estimated adult European exposure was near this value, with some groups higher.
9.establishes: The TWI is total weekly intake guidance, not a food-concentration ceiling. EFSA described individual kidney risk at estimated exposures as low while recommending population exposure reduction.
9.relevance: This supports concern about cumulative cadmium intake. HMTc still needs category-specific limits and consumption assumptions; a weekly body-weight allowance cannot directly decide a product’s composition.
